assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, brought fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and opened relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a path to redefining the second. This is the clearest case of a new measurement capability changing what can be observed, which is the criterion I weigh most.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye's group delivered the leading accuracy and stability demonstrations. Katori and Ye is a compact, defensible pair. Others (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Derevianko) contributed, and Ye is also credited on other candidates, but the supplied credit supports a two-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent clocks (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) have confirmed performance, and comparisons across continents are routine. Redefinition of the second is still pending, but the science is mature and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 precision-spectroscopy and frequency-comb recognition.
Whether ion clocks (Wineland group, already honored) and optical lattice clocks should be treated as separate achievements, and how to credit the broader community of contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into inertial sensors, gravimeters, gradiometers and tests of the equivalence principle and constants. It is a measurement technique with real instruments in the field, matching the view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers with gratings, Bordé gave the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich (with Chu) made the light-pulse interferometer into a precision sensor. Chu is not in the credited list and was recognized in 1997 for cooling, so the trio is workable but I would want to examine whether the credit omits key contributors such as Chu, Rasel and Peters. I am relying on memory for exact priority.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in many laboratories, with commercial and fieldable gravimeters and large-scale (10 m class) fountains. The field is mature, though the most ambitious applications such as gravitational-wave detection and dark-matter searches are still ahead.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested and complicated by the overlap with Chu's prior prize work and by laboratories (Chu, Peters, Rasel) not in the credited names.
The key sensitivity gains are incremental rather than a single decisive discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV centers in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor of magnetic field, temperature and strain, with uses from NMR on single molecules to biology. It matches both the quantum-information and the new-measurement-capability criteria.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first single-NV optical detection and coherent control; Lukin led the proposal and demonstration of NV quantum sensing and multi-qubit registers. Other prominent contributors (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth, Budker) are not in the credited list. A three-person grouping is plausible but boundary-sensitive.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many groups and moving into commercial sensors and early biological applications. Mature enough for recognition, though the sensing applications are still evolving and impact outside physics is real but not yet transformative.
uncertainties: Credit omits other groups that made decisive contributions such as Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby and Walsworth.
Lukin appears on other candidates, and sensing and qubit contributions may need to be split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized the Hubbard model and its relatives with tunable parameters, with the superfluid-Mott transition, quantum gas microscopes and single-site readout. It created an experimental platform for many-body physics that other fields now use, with strong lasting impact and clear experimental demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller supplied the theoretical proposal (Dalibard and Cirac contributed to the broader theory), Greiner and Bloch performed the landmark Mott-insulator experiment and Bloch led the microscopy and simulation developments. Five credited names exceed a prize, so a choice among them is unavoidable and contentious. Jaksch is not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Several groups have independently reproduced and extended the results, and the field is mature. Quantum simulation continues to grow, so recognition now is neither premature nor late.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among five names is unresolved, and some (Cirac, Dalibard) are strong alternatives.
Overlap with B001, B042 and B044 on Zoller and Cirac may split support for a single theme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Production and control of ultracold molecules, from buffer-gas cooling and magneto-optical trapping of molecules to quantum-state-resolved collisions and chemistry, opened precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment and new routes for quantum simulation. The measurement angle is strong, since molecular EDM limits constrain physics beyond the Standard Model.
assessment.attribution: Doyle (buffer-gas beams), DeMille (molecular trapping, ACME) and Ye (cold-molecule spectroscopy and KRb work, together with Jin who is not on the list) are plausible. Debbie Jin's death complicates the history, and several others (Meijer, Narevich, Nägerl, Ni) contributed to molecular cooling and control.
assessment.maturity: Direct laser cooling and trapping of molecules is still maturing, and applications such as eEDM bounds and quantum simulation with molecules are developing. Recognition seems a bit early compared with atoms.
uncertainties: The cluster of molecular cooling methods (buffer gas, Stark deceleration, laser cooling, association from atoms) may be too heterogeneous for a single prize.
The decisive scientific payoff, such as a new physics result or molecular quantum simulation, is not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire gain media and Kerr-lens and semiconductor-saturable-absorber mode-locking made tunable femtosecond lasers practical and widely available, and underlie frequency combs, attosecond science and multiphoton imaging. It is a classic enabling instrument, which is a kind of impact I value, although a large share of its downstream recognition has already come through earlier prizes.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed the Ti:sapphire laser, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking and Keller developed SESAMs. Priority in self-mode-locking and the roles of others (Spence, Kean, Sibbett) need care; I am relying on memory for the exact history.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use and many independent confirmations. Timing is late rather than early, which is not a negative for an instrument prize.
uncertainties: Much of the downstream impact has already been recognized in the 2018 and 2023 prizes and the frequency comb prize, which may dilute the case.
Credit is spread across a crystal, a mode-locking mechanism and a device, which may not form a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a bandstructure-engineered semiconductor laser with emission across the mid-infrared and terahertz ranges, now routine for trace-gas spectroscopy, sensing and metrology. It is a laser-spectroscopy instrument that opened a spectral region, which fits my experimental interests.
assessment.attribution: Faist, Capasso and colleagues at Bell Labs demonstrated the first device in 1994, with Cho's molecular-beam-epitaxy growth essential to realizing it. Others in the original team (Sirtori, Sivco, Hutchinson) are not credited, so the allocation is open. Kazarinov and Suris proposed the idea in 1971, which complicates priority.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed and commercialized, with continuous-wave room-temperature operation and many applications. Very mature, so timing is late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Priority history with the Kazarinov-Suris proposal and the other Bell Labs co-authors is unclear.
The discovery is more engineering than fundamental physics, which may weigh against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable tweezer arrays enable controllable many-body quantum simulators and gates with hundreds of qubits, and have yielded demonstrations of quantum phases and early error-corrected operations. The experimental control is impressive, but I would want to see long-term reproducibility and scaling beyond demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Lukin (blockade proposals and large-scale arrays), Browaeys (early blockade demonstration and tweezer arrays) and Saffman (gate proposals and demonstrations) are plausible. Zoller and Jaksch also made foundational proposals, and Weiss, Bernien, Endres and Greiner contributed to the tweezer experiments, so credit is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing; independent confirmation exists from several groups, but the field is still in flux and a prize might be premature relative to what the technology may become.
uncertainties: Recognition may be premature while platform scaling and error-correction results are evolving.
Credit allocation among theory proposals and experimental realizations is unresolved.
